messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Raymond is a 68-year-old married school counselor who has spent the better part of four decades helping adolescents navigate crisis. He presents now as someone in crisis himself, arriving at the intake appointment with the careful composure of a man who has spent years teaching others to name their feelings while remaining, in his own estimation, entirely unable to do so. His PCL-5 score of 62 places him in the severe range, and the clinical picture that emerges across the first few sessions is one of a man whose professional instincts toward connection have been systematically dismantled by what happened to him fourteen months ago.

The assault occurred late on a Friday evening in the parking lot of a bar Raymond had visited with a former colleague. He had not been drinking heavily — a detail he returns to with some bitterness — but the man who attacked him had been. Raymond remembers the smell before anything else: a sharp, sour wave of alcohol on the man's breath as he was shoved against a car door, then struck repeatedly. At some point he lost consciousness. He came around in an emergency room, the antiseptic sting of the air hitting him before he could open his eyes, a nurse leaning close and speaking in the careful, lowered voice people use when they are trying not to frighten you. He was badly concussed, had two broken ribs, and remained in hospital overnight. His wife held his hand. He does not remember much of that part.

What Raymond does remember, he remembers in pieces. He has described the assault not as a continuous narrative but as a sequence of still photographs: the yellow light of the parking lot, the man's face at close range, the specific angle of a fist. Each image arrives complete and discrete, and between them there is nothing — just the sensation of one frame cutting to the next. When a fragment surfaces without warning, as they frequently do, it carries with it the full physiological terror of the original moment: his heart rate spikes, his chest tightens, and for several seconds he is entirely certain he is about to be killed. The memory does not feel like recollection. It feels like recurrence.

The triggers that reliably summon these intrusions have shaped Raymond's daily life in ways that have become increasingly difficult to conceal. The smell of alcohol — encountered at faculty gatherings, at the occasional dinner where wine is poured nearby — sends a fragment crashing forward without warning, and Raymond has responded by withdrawing from most social occasions. He stopped attending the monthly staff dinners at his school, offering scheduling conflicts as explanation. More consequentially, the antiseptic smell of the school nurse's office, which sits two doors from his own, has become nearly intolerable; he now routes himself through a longer corridor to avoid passing it, and a colleague has noticed and asked, with genuine concern, whether he is all right. What troubles Raymond most acutely, however, is the trigger he finds hardest to explain: emotional closeness itself. When a student leans in to confide something painful, or when his wife reaches for him in the particular way she has when she senses he is struggling, something in him recoils. The proximity — the lowered voice, the attentive face — maps onto something in the assault he has not yet been able to articulate, and the memory surfaces.

In response, Raymond has developed a set of strategies that he recognises, with the rueful clarity of a trained counselor, as counterproductive. He avoids people where he can manage it, keeping sessions with students brief and professionally bounded. He has pulled back from his wife in ways that have produced a new and painful distance between them. And when avoidance is not possible — when someone gets emotionally close in a moment he cannot exit — he has learned to dissociate deliberately, to blank out behind attentive eyes, to be present in body while retreating entirely inward. The trouble is that this deliberate withdrawal keeps him in a state of vigilant watchfulness for the very cues he is trying to escape, so that the triggers remain perpetually salient, perpetually capable of pulling the next fragment forward.

What finally brought Raymond to seek help was a session three weeks ago in which a student described being attacked, and Raymond sat across from him, blank and unreachable, aware that he was failing the boy entirely. He came to his first appointment hoping, above all, to be able to do his job again. What he fears most is that the person who was good at it is gone.
